source_title: Remember Hema Malini vs Hema Malini? Alaska has a similar poll twist
source_excerpt:
In Alaska, Republican Senator Daniel Sullivan is fighting to retain his seat against Democrat Mary Peltola. But he has an unexpected namesake on the ballot: another Daniel Sullivan, who is a retired schoolteacher with no party affiliation.
India has seen its fair share of namesake candidates during elections. Sometimes they are independent candidates, occasionally they are suspected of being part of a strategy to confuse voters and split an opponent's support. They have provided plenty of material for election-season jokes, even as the candidates themselves have had serious business to attend to.
Remember Hema Malini versus Hema Malini in Mathura? Or Rahul Gandhi versus another Rahul Gandhi, and even a Raghul Gandhi, in Wayanad during the Lok Sabha elections?
Now, thousands of miles away, America has its own version of the same electoral spectacle. And this time, the joke is not quite landing with the man in the White House.
In Alaska, Republican Senator Daniel Sullivan is fighting to retain his seat against Democrat Mary Peltola. But he has an unexpected namesake on the ballot: another Daniel Sullivan, who is a retired schoolteacher with no party affiliation. WHEN A NAME BECOMES AN ELECTION STRATEGY
At first glance, it sounds like an ordinary candidate. After all, there is nothing inherently illegal about two people sharing a name and contesting the same election. But the second Sullivan's candidacy has turned into a political storm after The New York Times investigation reported that people connected to Peltola's campaign, along with Democratic operatives, spent months looking for candidates who could draw votes away from the Republican senator. Their search eventually led them to Daniel J Sullivan Jr, a retired schoolteacher from Petersburg.
The report described the exercise as a ballot-composition strategy, in which candidates are encouraged to enter a contest to alter the electoral arithmetic for a rival. The idea is simple: if voters mistake one candidate for another, even a small number of misplaced votes could matter in a close election.
There is, however, an important distinction between an allegation of political manoeuvring and proof of electoral fraud. Peltola's campaign has denied recruiting either Sullivan and said it has no involvement with their campaigns. Peltola herself dismissed the controversy as a distraction, saying voters were more concerned about everyday issues such as affordability and healthcare.
The retired teacher, too, has maintained that his campaign was independent.
But the story has now travelled far beyond the ballot paper. Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy ordered a state investigation into whether the alleged recruitment effort violated state law. The Justice Department has also expanded its criminal investigation, issuing more than 40 subpoenas and requests to preserve documents, including to the campaigns involved.
And Washington has gone a step further. The Justice Department has filed a separate lawsuit seeking to prevent Alaska from certifying the Senate result under certain circumstances if the Republican incumbent loses. The department argues that the second Sullivan's candidacy could confuse voters.
The Alaska Supreme Court has already allowed both candidates to remain on the ballot. The dispute, therefore, is no longer just about whether a namesake should be allowed to contest an election. It has become a test of how far federal authorities can go in challenging a state's election arrangements.
For US President Donald Trump , this was no harmless electoral coincidence. The US President saw an opportunity to turn a local ballot controversy into a national political battle, accusing Democrats of voter fraud and demanding that Peltola be removed from the ballot and prosecuted. WHY A SECOND DAN SULLIVAN COULD COST TRUMP DEARLY
WHY A SECOND DAN SULLIVAN COULD COST TRUMP DEARLY
There is a reason Trump is paying such close attention to what might otherwise have remained a local electoral curiosity.
The November 3 midterms will determine control of the US Congress, and Republicans are facing a difficult fight to retain both chambers. Losing the House would make life considerably harder for Trump. Losing the Senate as well could leave his administration facing an even more hostile Congress, with Democrats gaining greater power to investigate his policies, scrutinise his officials and obstruct his legislative priorities.
Alaska is particularly important because a race that would ordinarily be expected to favour Republicans has become competitive. Peltola, a former congresswoman and the first Alaska Native elected to the US House of Representatives, is challenging Sullivan in a contest that could influence the Senate balance.
The state's ranked-choice voting system adds another twist. Voters can rank candidates in order of preference, with lower-performing candidates eliminated and their votes transferred according to subsequent preferences. This could limit the impact of a namesake candidate, but it does not eliminate the possibility of confusion among voters who select the wrong Sullivan and fail to rank the incumbent as an alternative.
The second Sullivan received 2.5 per cent of the vote in Alaska's August primary, while the incumbent secured 41.4 per cent and Peltola received 49.5 per cent.
That may look like a small number, but in a close Senate race, even a handful of votes can become politically significant. And if Republicans lose the seat, Trump will have another controversy to point to. AMERICA'S ELECTORAL ODDITY HAS AN INDIAN PRECEDENT
AMERICA'S ELECTORAL ODDITY HAS AN INDIAN PRECEDENT
If the Alaska episode sounds unusual, Indian elections have produced some rather spectacular examples of the same phenomenon.
In the 2014 Mathura election, actor Hema Malini faced another candidate bearing the same name. In 2019, Rahul Gandhi encountered a namesake in Wayanad, along with another candidate whose name was spelt Raghul Gandhi.
The issue even reached the Supreme Court in 2024, when a public interest litigation challenged the practice of duplicate and namesake candidates. The court did not accept the argument that someone should be prevented from contesting simply because their name resembled that of a prominent political leader.
That is the democratic dilemma at the heart of the Alaska controversy. A candidate cannot simply be barred because he happens to share a name with someone more famous. At the same time, deliberately exploiting that similarity to mislead voters, if established, raises a different set of legal and ethical problems. - Ends With inputs from PTI
